entry.title: [推荐] Rethinking (De)growth: the politics of compost
entry.content:
Contemporary Political Theory · Vol. 25 No. 1 · 推荐 (5.0)

Jessica Croteau

Moving beyond economic analyses of degrowth, growth and consumption are reframed through decomposition as a vital process through which life, value, and politics are continually re-composed. Against dominant imaginaries that cast decay as waste or ruination, this article turns to composting and carrion ecologies to articulate decomposition as a generative undoing and a mode of transformation that binds waste to worth. Drawing on multispecies examples from vultures in India to the Baltimore Compost Collective, the article situates decomposition as both material process and political metaphor to enact a revaluation of growth, decay, and consumption that unsettles capitalist logics of extraction and accumulation. entry.title: [推荐] The subject of intelligence: AI as existential risk and the government of the human and the future
entry.content:
Contemporary Political Theory · Vol. 25 No. 1 · 推荐 (5.0)

Caio Simoneti

This article analyses discourses on artificial intelligence (AI) in the field of existential risk studies. AI appears as a key theme in existential risk circles, not only as a source of risk, but also as a resource for risk prevention and as the enabler of a glorious future for humanity. However, what is it about AI that brings together utopian and dystopian imaginaries? Why is a discourse on AI so tied to questions regarding the human, and what forms of humanity does it produce? What forms of governing does it enable? This article argues that the concept of ‘intelligence’ is fundamental regarding both how AI is construed as an existential risk, as well as how humanity is conceptualised as that which needs to be protected. entry.title: [推荐] From universalism to situated universality: reconfiguring Kantian pacifism
entry.content:
Contemporary Political Theory · Vol. 25 No. 1 · 推荐 (5.0)

Naomi Ellis

In Toward Perpetual Peace , Kant argues that war’s violence enables humanity to envision perpetual peace as both reason’s moral end and history’s presumptive telos, thereby motivating action to renounce war. This article critiques the universalist assumption underlying this argument and argues instead for a pacifism grounded in what I call ‘situated universality’. I do so through a comparative political theoretical approach. After reconstructing Kant’s account of peace, I turn to post-World War II Japan, where a Kantian defense of its pacifist constitution initially flourished, but was later challenged by a nationalistic counter-discourse. entry.title: [推荐] Difference‐Making Under Metaphysical Indeterminacy
entry.content:
Philosophy & Public Affairs · Vol. 54 No. 4 262-273 · 推荐 (4.0)

Jessica Li

Many of the most pressing moral problems we face involve collective harms generated by large numbers of individually insignificant actions. Unlike triggering cases—where a threshold exists such that a single act could be decisive—non‐triggering cases lack any such sharp cutoff. In these cases, no individual act appears to make a difference to whether harm occurs, and it may be metaphysically indeterminate whether a given aggregate is harmful or whether a marginal contribution plays any causal role at all. I argue that standard approaches to moral responsibility, which rely on difference‐making or expected outcomes, struggle to provide action‐guiding reasons in these contexts. entry.title: [推荐] Is religion a problem for intersectional theory? Muslim women, feminism, and varieties of patriarchy
entry.content:
Contemporary Political Theory · Vol. 25 No. 1 · 推荐 (3.0)

Karolin I. M. Tuncel、Tobias Müller

Intersectional theory has been criticised for neglecting religion and for being unable to account for religion’s social complexities. This contribution interrogates this critique by disaggregating different relationships of Muslim women to secular and religious varieties of patriarchy. We argue that what demarcates the challenges of intersectional analysis are the political contestations not around religion, but around women’s pro-patriarchal agency. We do so by discussing intersectional theory’s analytical usefulness and limitations in conceptualising the experiences of Muslim women. entry.title: [推荐] Democracy, History, (Counter-)Institution: Castoriadis and the Radical Imagination
entry.content:
Theory, Culture & Society · 预印(online-first) · 推荐 (6.0)

Sara Gebh、Sergej Seitz

Some 50 years after Cornelius Castoriadis’s The Imaginary Institution of Society (1975), this special section asks what his thought can contribute to a present marked by the crisis of democracy. The crisis is at heart a crisis of political and democratic imagination: of our capacity to collectively shape the common world and envisage democratic alternatives to the status quo. Reading Castoriadis with and beyond himself, the special section focuses on his accounts of democratic autonomy, the imaginary institution of society, and history as creation, while contesting the Eurocentric, anti-representational, and apriorist limits of his thought. Across three registers (imaginaries, histories, and institutions), the contributions envisage a plural, historically grounded, and decidedly political account of the institutions through which collective self-institution and imagination are kept alive

entry.title: [推荐] A Footnote to Nietzsche: Carlo Ginzburg on Michel Foucault, and his 1964 review of Histoire de la folie
entry.content:
Theory, Culture & Society · 预印(online-first) · 推荐 (5.0)

Stuart Elden、Federico Testa

Marking both the passing of Italian historian Carlo Ginzburg (1939–2026) and the centenary of Michel Foucault’s birth (1926–84), this article presents a translation of a largely unknown 1964 review by Carlo Ginzburg of Michel Foucault’s first major book, History of Madness . It was written when Ginzburg was in his mid-20s, before his first books, and originally published in the Italian journal Studi Medievali . The review articulates the young historian’s main criticisms of Foucault’s project, which will form the basis of his later assessment of Foucault. The translation is introduced by a detailed discussion of Ginzburg’s lifelong engagement with Foucault. It particularly focuses on his critique of History of Madness as about the act of exclusion rather than those excluded.

Historical Materialism · 1-33 · 预印(online-first) · 必读 (12.0)

Daniel Andrés López

Published in 1948, Lukács’s work The Young Hegel is a monumental and largely overlooked study of Hegel’s early writing. This article argues that the book should be read as part of Lukács’s ‘orthodox Marxist’ period, and as an attempt to develop a more rigorous Marxist philosophy in opposition to the mistakes the author perceived in his earlier philosophy of praxis. Beyond that, this essay argues that Lukács develops a powerful implicit critique of Stalinist Marxism and the state bureaucracy underlying it via a reconstruction of Hegel’s account of the development of Christianity into a positive state religion. Subsequently, this essay defends Hegel against Lukács’s critique, suggesting that the Marxism outlined in The Young Hegel is conceptually and historically abstract. Patricia Cipollitti Rodríguez

The decolonial category of exteriority indexes communities in which people think, act, and feel “otherwise” to Western capitalist modernity. Recent proposals to decolonize critical theory have recognized the methodological importance of theorizing from exteriorities as sites of exclusion. In this article, I evaluate exteriority and, specifically, whether this idea ignores the realities of capitalist globalization. After explaining the role that exteriority plays in analectical critique, which is proposed as a non‐Eurocentric alternative to critical theory's dialectical methods, I assess two versions of the concern that decolonial criticism romanticizes and distorts social reality. entry.title: [必读] Populism and Recognition
entry.content:
Constellations · 预印(online-first) · 必读 (7.5)

Cillian McBride

Populist resentment is ostensibly rooted in elite misrecognition of the virtues of the ordinary people. This suggests a relatively benign view of populist recognition struggle. This paper suggests an alternative, more complex, reading, focusing on the dimension of normative authority always present in recognition claims. This suggests that populist resentment is primarily rooted in claims to superior social status and authority. Populist recognition struggles have two important dimensions—remedying a recognition deficit by constituting themselves as the “real people” and simultaneously defying the authority of the liberal elite. Finally, the normative authority view traces the well‐known insecurity of populists to the self‐defeating character of their assertion of the unlimited authority of the will of the people.
